## Recognise a perfect-square trinomial

Identify the squares at each end. Check that the middle term equals twice the product of their bases, with the appropriate sign.

:::::: {.example-pair}

::::: {.model}

<h3>Worked example</h3>

$9x^2-30x+25$

::: {.fragment}

[Identify the squares.]{.annotation}

$9x^2=(3x)^2$ and $25=5^2$.

:::

::: {.fragment}

[Check the middle term.]{.annotation}

$-2(3x)(5)=-30x$

:::

::: {.fragment}

[Use the minus sign inside the bracket.]{.annotation}

$9x^2-30x+25=(3x-5)^2$

:::

:::::

::::: {.paper}

::: {.fragment}

<h3>Your turn</h3>

$9x^2+30x+25$

Factorise on paper. Which sign changes?

:::

::: {.fragment}

[Check your working]{.annotation}

$2(3x)(5)=30x$, so the factorisation is $(3x+5)^2$.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**Quick check.** Is $9x^2+29x+25$ a perfect square? Decide before selecting Next.

:::

::: {.fragment}

The middle term would have to be $30x$. The $29x$ rules out a perfect square.

:::
